summary: An FYI document that collects answers to common questions asked by new Internet users, produced by the User Services Working Group. It is FYI 4 and informational. It was replaced by RFC 1206.

eli5.summary: A list of questions new people ask about the Internet, with answers.

questions: new internet user questions and answers
subtitle: Answers to the most commonly asked questions by new Internet users.

tldr.problem: New Internet users often ask the same basic questions about what the Internet is, how to use its services, and where to find information.
tldr.mechanism: The User Services Working Group collected frequently asked questions and wrote clear, concise answers covering the Internet itself, TCP/IP protocols, documentation, organizations, services, and a detailed glossary of networking terms.
tldr.outcome: This FYI provided a valuable reference for new users joining the early Internet. It was later superseded by RFC 1206, which updated the Q&A collection.

today: RFC 1177 is Informational and was superseded by RFC 1206, which provides updated answers and questions for new Internet users.

sections.title: Getting Started on the Internet
sections.content:
When you first join the Internet, you gain access to resources on your own computer, any other Internet computer where you have an account, and any publicly accessible computer on the Internet. You can transfer files using FTP, log into other computers interactively, and send electronic mail to anyone with an Internet address or access to Internet-connected email systems.

The Internet Resource Guide, published by the NSF Network Service Center, lists supercomputer centers, library catalogs, archives and specialized databases available to you. Additional services include email directories, WHOIS lookups for finding hosts and people, and service location protocols for discovering available services.
sections.eli5: The Internet lets you copy files from other computers, log in remotely, send mail, and find information on public databases around the world.

sections.title: Internet Basics and TCP/IP
sections.content:
TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) is the family of protocols that ties computers and networks together into the Internet. TCP/IP originated on ARPANET and is now used internationally by universities, research institutions, governments, and some corporations.

The main protocols in the TCP/IP suite are TCP (for reliable ordered streams), IP (for routing packets), SMTP (for mail transfer), FTP (for file transfer), and Telnet (for remote login). Many other protocols extend the suite for specialized purposes. The Internet Activities Board publishes the state of standardization and recommended usage of all Internet protocols.
sections.eli5: TCP/IP is the rulebook that all computers on the Internet follow. It includes rules for sending mail, copying files, logging in, and many other things.

sections.title: Internet Organizations and How to Get Help
sections.content:
The Internet Activities Board (IAB) is the coordinating committee for Internet design, engineering, and management. It manages the RFC publication process and oversees two major task forces: the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) for near-term protocol issues, and the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) for long-term research.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) coordinates the use of protocol parameters: op-codes, type fields, port numbers, protocol numbers, and assigned system names. The Network Information Center (NIC) at the Defense Data Network is the primary repository for RFCs and Internet drafts, provides WHOIS database services, and maintains the Internet Registry (IR), which assigns network numbers and Autonomous System numbers.
sections.eli5: The Internet has organizations that make decisions, manage numbering systems, and keep the rulebooks. The NIC is like the central library where you can find everything.

sections.title: Using Internet Services
sections.content:
Email directories: Two major directories exist: the WHOIS database at the DDN NIC (accessible via Telnet to NIC.DDN.MIL) and the PSInet White Pages (at WP.PSI.COM). Both are incomplete, and it is still often necessary to ask people directly for their email addresses.

Usenet and Netnews: A distributed bulletin board system that some Internet computers participate in (though not all Usenet sites are on the Internet). To join Usenet, you need software (often available free via FTP) and a connection to an existing Usenet site.

Anonymous FTP: A way to access public files on other computers. Login with username 'anonymous' and password 'guest' to retrieve files from FTP servers worldwide.
sections.eli5: The Internet has directories for finding people, bulletin boards for discussions, and ways to copy files from public computers.

sections.title: Understanding RFCs and Documentation
sections.content:
RFCs (Request for Comments) are the working notes of the Internet research and development community. They may cover any topic related to computer communication: meeting reports, protocol specifications, policy studies, or technical committee work. Most RFCs describe network protocols and services with detailed procedures and formats.

RFCs receive technical review but are not refereed publications. Standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards. Once assigned an RFC number, a document is never revised or re-issued with the same number; if a protocol is improved, it gets a new RFC number. The IAB Official Protocol Standards document (currently RFC 1140) lists which RFC to use for each current protocol.

RFCs can be obtained via anonymous FTP from NIC.DDN.MIL or NIS.NSF.NET, or via email request if FTP is unavailable.
sections.eli5: RFCs are the Internet's instruction manuals. Once published, they never change, but new versions of protocols get new RFC numbers. You can download them from computers on the Internet.

sections.title: Networking Terms and Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC includes an extensive glossary defining common Internet terms. Key concepts include:

Networking basics: Packets (units of data sent across networks), datagrams (the unit transmitted between Internet modules), protocols (formal descriptions of message formats and exchange rules), and gateways (computers that connect multiple networks and route packets between them).

Addresses and routing: Network number (the part of an IP address designating the network), host number (the part designating the node), subnet number (for subdividing networks), and default routes (for forwarding traffic to unknown destinations).

Common networks and services: LANs (local area networks), Ethernet standards, X.25 protocols, and services like NFS (network file systems) and RPC (remote procedure calls) for distributed computing.
sections.eli5: The RFC explains hundreds of networking words: from simple terms like 'packet' (a bundle of data) to complex concepts like routing (finding the path to send data).
